desc:
The string s contains lowercase letters and the parentheses '(' and ')'. You want to make its parentheses well-formed by deleting as few parentheses as possible. Letters must never be deleted, and the relative order of the remaining characters stays the same.

Among all ways to do this with the minimum number of deletions, different choices of positions may produce the same string. Return the number of distinct resulting strings.

For example, "()())()" needs 1 deletion and can become "()()()" or "(())()", so the answer is 2. The string ")(" becomes the empty string only, so the answer is 1.
hints: First find out how many ')' and how many '(' have to be deleted at least. A single left-to-right scan with a counter gives both numbers.
Now search: at every parenthesis you may keep it or delete it, as long as you do not delete more than you are allowed to, and you prune as soon as the running balance goes negative.

To avoid counting equal strings many times, when you delete a parenthesis from a run of identical consecutive parentheses, always delete the first one in the run that you still have a choice about. Collect the finished strings in a set to be safe and return its size.
editorial: A scan with a balance counter finds the minimum deletions: every ')' met when the balance is 0 must be deleted (r of them), and the balance left at the end is the number of '(' to delete (l). Any solution that deletes more than this is not minimal, so we only look for strings reachable with exactly l deleted openings and r deleted closings.

Run a depth-first search over positions with the remaining budgets l, r and the current balance. At a parenthesis, either delete it (when that budget is positive) or keep it (and update the balance, rejecting a negative balance). Deleting the same character at different places of a run of equal characters gives the same string, so skip the deletion at index i when s[i] == s[i-1] and that previous character was kept: this makes deletions within a run happen at its start. The search can still reach the same string through different branches, so the finished strings are stored in a set whose size is the answer. With at most 20 parentheses the search space is small (a few ten thousand states in the worst case).
